title: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring Down
goal: I can divide a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number with long division, one step at a time.

card.desc: Bailey learns long division on Zoom: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, and repeat. She shares dimes and pennies to see why we divide the tens first, estimates before she divides, and solves 2-digit problems like 96 ÷ 6 with no remainder, one step at a time. Seven new words, including place value and methodical.

win: You did long division, one step at a time. Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down!

slides.title: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring Down
slides.text: Today you learn long division: a way to divide numbers that are too big for one fact. You will do it one step at a time, and every step is a fact you already know.

notes.do: Share your screen. Before you start, check that Bailey has at her table: 9 dimes and about 40 pennies (or 9 paper strips for tens and 40 beans for ones), 6 paper plates, paper, a pencil and her book. Keep your whiteboard in view of your camera.
notes.say: "On Thursday you showed me you kept your facts. Today those facts become a brand-new tool. If it looks big, remember: it is just one small step at a time, and I will be right here for every step."
notes.ask: "How many 4s fit in 8?" (2). "Hold on to that. It is the very first step today."

slides.title: Back to Berk
slides.text: Think about How to Train Your Dragon.
prompts: Tell what happened in the part you read this weekend, in order: first, next, then, last.
Stoick is Hiccup's father and the leader of the tribe. How does Stoick feel about Hiccup? Give one clue from the book.
Training Toothless is hard, but Hiccup keeps trying. Why might slow, careful work beat rushing?
starters: Slow, careful work beats rushing because …

notes.do: 6 minutes. Let her hold up the book to the camera and read a line if she wants.
notes.ask: "How does Stoick feel about Hiccup? What clue tells you?"
notes.listen: A feeling backed by a clue from the text. The last prompt is a bridge to today: slow, careful, step-by-step work beats rushing. Say so: "That is exactly how long division works."

slides.text: Say the answer out loud. Jonathan types it.

notes.do: She says each answer; you type it (she cannot type on your screen on Zoom).
notes.say: Praise each right answer: "Yes! That is a step from today's first problem."
notes.listen: The middle one is the key idea: "How many fit" can be a number that does not divide evenly. If she says 9 ÷ 6 doesn't work, ask: "How many WHOLE 6s fit?"

slides.title: Words for today
slides.text: Read each card out loud. Then use the word in your own sentence.

words.meaning: A way to divide big numbers one place at a time with four steps: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.
What a digit is worth because of where it sits: ones, tens or hundreds.
words.example: In 84, the 8 has a place value of 8 tens, which is 80.

words.meaning: In long division, to move the next digit of the dividend down next to what is left.
words.example: After you subtract, bring down the next digit.

words.meaning: The order that things happen in.
words.example: The sequence is divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.

words.meaning: Doing things carefully, one step at a time, in order.
words.example: A methodical mathematician never skips a step.

words.meaning: The leader of a tribe or clan.
words.example: Stoick, Hiccup's father, is the chieftain of the Hairy Hooligan Tribe.

words.meaning: Careful to avoid mistakes or danger.
words.example: A cautious Viking tests the ice before walking on it.

notes.do: Flip one card at a time on your screen. She reads the word and meaning aloud. Write Divide · Multiply · Subtract · Bring down on your whiteboard and keep it on camera all lesson.
notes.say: "Three long-division words, one word about order, and three story words. Methodical is how we will work today."
notes.ask: "Who is the chieftain of the Hairy Hooligans?" (Stoick.) "Tell me something you are cautious about." "What is the place value of the 9 in 96?" (9 tens, or 90.)
notes.listen: For methodical: careful, in order, no skipping. For sequence: the order of steps.

slides.title: Share it by place value
slides.text: There is no times-table fact for 84 ÷ 4. So we split 84 by place value: 8 tens and 4 ones.

steps.text: Share the tens first: 8 dimes on 4 plates. Each plate gets 2 dimes (2 tens).
Now share the ones: 4 pennies on 4 plates. Each plate gets 1 penny (1 one).
Each plate has 2 tens and 1 one: 21. So 84 ÷ 4 = 21.

slides.tip: Long division works the same way: tens first, then ones.

notes.do: Hands-on at home: she sets out 4 plates, 8 dimes and 4 pennies, and deals the dimes first, then the pennies. Hold each step until she has done it with her coins.
notes.ask: "How much money is on each plate?" (21 cents.) "Why did we share the dimes first?" (Biggest place first.)
notes.listen: She sees that each plate has 2 dimes and 1 penny. Praise: "You just did long division with coins!"

slides.title: Estimate first
slides.text: Before you divide, decide about how big the answer will be. Multiply the divisor by 10, 20, 30…

steps.text: 84 ÷ 4. 4 × 20 = 80. 84 is a little more than 80, so the answer is a little more than 20.
96 ÷ 6. 6 × 10 = 60 and 6 × 20 = 120. 96 is between 60 and 120, so the answer is between 10 and 20.

slides.tip: If your answer is not near your estimate, check your steps.

notes.listen: She multiplies by tens to bracket the answer. That is the place-value sense that catches a dropped digit later.

slides.title: The four steps
slides.text: Long division repeats four steps in the same sequence until there are no digits left to bring down.

visual.sub: Memory trick: Dad, Mom, Sister, Brother

steps.text: Divide: how many times does the divisor fit? Write that digit in the quotient.
Multiply: that digit × the divisor. Write the product underneath.
Subtract: find what is left. It must be smaller than the divisor.
Bring down: move the next digit down. Then start again with Divide.

notes.say: "Dad, Mom, Sister, Brother. Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down. Say it with me."
notes.ask: "Which step uses the remainder rule from Thursday?" (Subtract: what is left must be smaller than the divisor.)
notes.listen: She can say the four steps in order without looking. Have her say them three times, faster each time.

slides.title: 84 ÷ 4: the tens
slides.text: Tap Show me the next step. One step at a time.

steps.text: Divide. How many 4s fit in 8? 2 (4 × 2 = 8). Write 2 above the 8 in the tens place.
Multiply. 2 × 4 = 8. Write 8 under the 8.
Subtract. 8 − 8 = 0. Check: 0 is smaller than 4.

notes.do: Before each click, ask her to say the step and the number. Then click to show it. On paper at home, she copies each step as it appears.
notes.say: Praise each correct step right away: "Yes, divide: 2!" "Right, 2 × 4 = 8." "Perfect, nothing left."
notes.ask: "Why does the 2 go above the 8 and not above the 4?" (It is 2 tens, so it goes in the tens place.)
notes.listen: She names the step before the number. If she freezes, point to the whiteboard: "Which step comes after divide?"

slides.title: 84 ÷ 4: the ones
slides.text: Keep going. Bring down, then the same steps again.

steps.text: Bring down. Bring down the 4 from the ones place. The 0 and the 4 make 04, which is just 4.
Divide. How many 4s fit in 4? 1 (4 × 1 = 4). Write 1 above the 4 in the ones place.
Multiply. 1 × 4 = 4. Write 4 under the 4.
Subtract. 4 − 4 = 0. Check: 0 is smaller than 4. There are no more digits to bring down, so 84 ÷ 4 = 21.
Check by multiplying. 21 × 4 = 84. It matches, so 84 ÷ 4 = 21 is right.

slides.tip: The answer matches your estimate (a little more than 20).

notes.do: Same routine: she says it, you click, she writes it.
notes.say: Praise every step: "Bring down, yes!" "1, yes!" Then: "You just finished your first long division. 21 is a little more than 20, just like your estimate."
notes.ask: "Why did we bring down the 4?" (There was a digit left at the top.)

slides.title: What comes next?
slides.text: Look at the work. Say which step comes next. Jonathan taps it.

items.q: 68 ÷ 2. Look at the work so far. Which step comes next?
items.why: You just wrote a digit in the quotient. Now multiply it by the divisor.
no: You divide right after you bring down a new digit, or at the very start.
You subtract right after you write the product underneath.
You bring down right after you subtract, when a digit is still waiting.

items.q: 93 ÷ 3. Look at the work so far. Which step comes next?
items.why: You subtracted and there is still a digit up top that has not been used. Bring it down.
no: You divide right after you bring down a new digit, or at the very start.
You multiply right after you write a new digit in the quotient.
You subtract right after you write the product underneath.

items.q: 76 ÷ 4. What digit goes in the quotient next?
items.why: How many 4s fit in 36? 9, because 4 × 9 = 36.

notes.do: She answers out loud; you tap or type for her.
notes.ask: After each: "How do you know?" ("I just wrote a digit up top, so I multiply.")
notes.listen: She reads the LAST thing written to decide the next step. On 76 ÷ 4, the digit is 9: 4 × 9 = 36. If she says 8, ask: "Is anything left if you use 8? Is it smaller than 4?"

slides.title: 96 ÷ 6: the tens
slides.text: This time something is left over after the tens.

steps.text: Divide. How many 6s fit in 9? 1 (6 × 1 = 6; 6 × 2 = 12 is too big). Write 1 above the 9 in the tens place.
Multiply. 1 × 6 = 6. Write 6 under the 9.
Subtract. 9 − 6 = 3. Check: 3 is smaller than 6.

notes.do: Hands-on at home: 9 dimes on 6 plates. Each plate gets 1 dime; 3 dimes are left in her hand.
notes.say: Praise each step: "1, yes!" "6, yes!" "3 left, and 3 is smaller than 6. Perfect."
notes.ask: "What are the 3 left over: 3 ones or 3 tens?" (3 tens: three dimes.)
notes.listen: She sees the 3 are tens. That is why we bring the ones down next to them.

slides.title: 96 ÷ 6: the ones
slides.text: Bring down the 6. The 3 tens and 6 ones make 36.

steps.text: Bring down. Bring down the 6 from the ones place. Now you have 36.
Divide. How many 6s fit in 36? 6 (6 × 6 = 36). Write 6 above the 6 in the ones place.
Multiply. 6 × 6 = 36. Write 36 under the 36.
Subtract. 36 − 36 = 0. Check: 0 is smaller than 6. There are no more digits to bring down, so 96 ÷ 6 = 16.
Check by multiplying. 16 × 6 = 60 + 36 = 96. It matches!

slides.tip: 16 is between 10 and 20, just like the estimate.

notes.do: Hands-on: she trades her 3 dimes for 30 pennies, adds the 6 pennies (36 pennies), and deals them onto the 6 plates: 6 each. Each plate: 1 dime + 6 pennies = 16 cents.
notes.say: Praise each step out loud. At the end: "Look at your plates. 16 cents each. The coins and the long division say the same thing."
notes.ask: "Where did the 36 come from?" (3 tens left + 6 ones = 36 ones.)

slides.title: 72 ÷ 3, step by step
slides.text: Say the steps in order. Jonathan taps them.
steps: Divide: 3 fits in 7 two times. Write 2.
Bring down the 2. Now you have 12.
Divide: 3 fits in 12 four times. Write 4.
slides.why: Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, then again. 72 ÷ 3 = 24.
slides.hint: Start with Divide. After you subtract, bring down.

notes.do: She says which card comes next; you tap it. Then she writes the whole problem on her paper and holds it up to the camera.
notes.say: Praise each card: "Yes, multiply comes after divide."
notes.listen: On the paper: the 2 above the 7, the 4 above the 2, and the 12 lined up under the 12.

teacher.objective: Bailey learns the long division sequence (divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, repeat) and what each step means in place value (tens first, then ones; tens left over join the ones when you bring down). She estimates first by multiplying the divisor by tens, and solves 2-digit ÷ 1-digit problems with no remainder (84 ÷ 4, 96 ÷ 6, 72 ÷ 3), checking by multiplying.
materials: Zoom: share your screen with the Class lesson (teacher code 9110)
Whiteboard and marker (Jonathan), visible on camera, with the four steps written on it
At Bailey's home (ask Tia to set out before the lesson): 9 dimes and about 40 pennies (or 9 paper strips for tens and 40 beans for ones), 6 paper plates
Paper and a pencil for Bailey; she holds her work up to the camera
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Packet (2 pages): printed later this week; it is assigned on Tuesday's task list

plan.do: Class slide 1. Confirm dimes, pennies, plates, paper and pencil are at her table. Quick fact: how many 4s fit in 8?
Class slide 2. Retell in order, how Stoick feels about Hiccup with a clue, why step by step beats rushing.
Class slide 3. Three facts she needs today; she says them, you type.
Class slide 4. She reads each card and makes her own sentence. The four steps go on your whiteboard.
Class slides 5–6. 8 dimes and 4 pennies onto 4 plates (21 cents each); estimate 84 ÷ 4 and 96 ÷ 6 by multiplying by tens.
Class slides 7–9. Dad, Mom, Sister, Brother; then 84 ÷ 4 one step at a time. She says each step before you click, writes it on paper, and you praise each correct step.
Class slide 10. She reads the last thing written and names the next step or digit.
Class slides 11–12. 9 dimes onto 6 plates, 3 dimes left, trade for 30 pennies, add 6, deal 36: 16 cents each. Long division step by step alongside the coins.
Class slide 13. 72 ÷ 3: she says the order, you tap; she writes it and shows it to the camera.
Class slide 14. 75 ÷ 5, 92 ÷ 4, 91 ÷ 7 on paper; she leads the steps, you praise each one.
Class slide 16. Methodical, place value, bring down; cautious in her own sentence.
Class slide 17. 78 ÷ 6, 84 ÷ 7, 87 ÷ 3 alone on paper; note any skipped step.
Class slide 18. Course page: tonight the After-class lesson (needs 90) and 10 minutes of reading; the Pathways reading on Tuesday or Wednesday.

watch: Writing the first quotient digit above the wrong place (above the ones). Ask: "Is that 2 tens or 2 ones? Where do tens go?"
Skipping the bring-down and dividing only the leftover (in 96 ÷ 6, dividing 3 ÷ 6). Point to the whiteboard: "After subtract comes…?"
A leftover that is as big as or bigger than the divisor (writing 1 in 92 ÷ 4 and leaving 5). Ask: "Is 5 smaller than 4? Could another 4 fit?"
Losing the place in the sequence. Have her touch the step on her paper and say it before writing.
Adding the divisor over and over to find how many fit (4, 8, 12 …). Ask for the fact instead: "4 times what is close to 12?"
"I can't do it." Do not explain the whole problem. Ask only: "What is the first step?" When she does it, praise that one step, then ask for the next.

packet_key.answer: long division → dividing one place at a time; place value → what a digit is worth because of where it sits; bring down → move the next digit down; sequence → the order things happen in; methodical → one step at a time, in order; chieftain → the leader of a tribe; cautious → careful to avoid mistakes or danger
Answers vary. Example: I share the 8 tens first, 2 tens each, then the 4 ones, 1 each, so 84 ÷ 4 = 21. I am methodical and do one step at a time.
39 (2 into 7 three times, 1 left, bring down 8: 18 ÷ 2 = 9). Check: 39 × 2 = 78
25 (3 into 7 twice, 1 left, bring down 5: 15 ÷ 3 = 5). Check: 25 × 3 = 75
46 (2 into 9 four times, 1 left, bring down 2: 12 ÷ 2 = 6). Check: 46 × 2 = 92
15 (4 into 6 once, 2 left, bring down 0: 20 ÷ 4 = 5). Check: 15 × 4 = 60
Answers vary; uses chieftain correctly and gives a reason from the book.

teacher.notes: The class lesson ends at the wrap-up; Bailey takes Show What You Know on her own tonight at the end of the After-class lesson. Check her Formspree score before Tuesday. If it is under 90, open Tuesday's class with 10 minutes of 2-digit long division with coins (try 72 ÷ 3 and 85 ÷ 5), saying each step out loud, then have her retake (she gets a brand-new question set). Monday's practice set and packet are on Tuesday's task list, not tonight's. Tuesday builds directly on today: the same four steps with 3-digit numbers.
